nodes.label: Causal mandate audit
nodes.description: A specified comparison of how permissible delegate policies change future typed action scope under an unchanged authentic adaptive delegation rule.

nodes.label: Conditional influence contract
nodes.description: A conditional grant specification that states which intervention classes may contribute evidence to updates of the delegate’s own action scope.

nodes.label: Typed scope contrast
nodes.description: An explicit comparison of permissions added, removed, or changed across policies, preserving action, resource, purpose, recipients, budget, duration, and jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Authority ancestry
nodes.description: The trace from an action’s permission through its grant, update rule, evidence history, and any subdelegation.

nodes.label: Synthetic scope contrast
nodes.description: A constructed result, not a human finding.

nodes.label: Performative prediction
nodes.description: Known distribution feedback. Our audit inherits this ancestry.

nodes.label: Measurement construction
nodes.description: The original case changes suggestion-match counts, not chosen options.

nodes.label: Randomized policy study
nodes.description: A proposed test. No experiment has been run.

nodes.label: Recovery after assistance
nodes.description: The capabilities, alternatives, and transition costs available after a person or institution reduces reliance on assistance.

nodes.label: Preference pollution
nodes.description: System recommendations can influence the later preference evidence used to evaluate or update the system.

nodes.label: Artificial welfare uncertainty
nodes.description: Uncertainty about artificial moral patienthood motivates distinct assessment and lifecycle questions without establishing that present systems possess welfare.

nodes.label: Qualified mandate
nodes.description: A permission set identifying who may act for whom, on which resources, for what purpose, within which bounds.

nodes.label: Audit the evidence that updates authority
nodes.description: Authenticate the grant; replay the exact rule; estimate or bound the total intervention-policy contrast in typed future scope; return governance judgment separately.

nodes.label: Specify the terms of chosen change
nodes.description: Do not equate influence with illegitimacy. Bind formation purpose, intervention classes, scope criteria, review triggers, and locally valid ratification procedures when conditional authority depends on human-state signals.

nodes.label: Evaluate what remains after help
nodes.description: Measure assisted success, transfer capacity, alternatives, review burden, and shared-resource effects separately. Treat access needs and chosen dependence explicitly. Keep artificial welfare uncertainty analytically distinct.

nodes.label: Behavioral criterion is the mediator in the fixture
nodes.description:
Replacing accepted-suggestion count with independent task-success count yields
equal final scopes in the fixture. This is an ablation of that construction,
not a field-validated causal mechanism in human populations.

nodes.label: Synthetic coaching counterexample
nodes.description:
A declared chosen-coaching purpose can accompany positive scope sensitivity.
Therefore policy sensitivity alone cannot entail a verdict of manipulation.
The fixture declaration does not validate real informed consent.

nodes.label: Scalar growth condition
nodes.description:
Under constant latent state, a centered noiseless linear behavioral score and
the specified saturated scalar rule, local growth occurs when `kbc > rho`.
This is elementary recurrence analysis, not a new control theorem.

nodes.label: Four-output audit
nodes.description: Report integrity, rule conformance, policy sensitivity, and governance as separate outputs for adaptive mandates.

nodes.label: Logical independence of integrity, conformance, and sensitivity
nodes.description: Integrity and exact rule conformance do not imply zero policy sensitivity.

nodes.label: Acceptance-criterion contrast
nodes.description: When a scope rule counts acceptance of the system's own highlighted recommendation, changing the highlighting policy will change the probability of a widening transition more than it changes independent task-success criteria.

nodes.label: Adaptive scope trajectory contrast
nodes.description: Adaptive delegation based on agent-sensitive criteria produces different scope trajectories from delegation based on externally measured performance, even when immediate utility is similar.

nodes.label: Review-burden contrast
nodes.description: Frequent beneficiary-controlled review prompts increase approval while reducing attention and comprehension relative to batched, principal-controlled review.

nodes.label: Immediate-source handoff loss
nodes.description: If a handoff schema preserves only immediate source, then a truthful intermediate signature can hide a policy ancestor material to the authorization decision.

nodes.label: Separate ancestry from predictive relevance
nodes.description: An authorization service should not treat source authenticity or predictive relevance as sufficient for a widening transition when the prospective beneficiary materially controls causal ancestors of the evidence. It should record that ancestry and apply an influence policy or route the transition to review.

nodes.label: Reference widening procedure
nodes.description: For a proposed widening transition: authenticate the grant and evidence envelopes; validate role and jurisdiction separately from signature origin; replay the rule and enumerate exact added, removed, and incomparable permissions; retrieve evidence provenance and ancestry; evaluate the total policy contrast or declare it unidentified; check whether a prior grant governed the relevant influence and bounded the successor scope; when required, keep the prior valid scope while offering review through a refusal-capable channel; execute only the resulting authorized actions; and preserve scope attenuation, ancestry status, revocation, and appeal through subdelegation.

nodes.label: Refusal-capable widening review
nodes.description: Review for widening should preserve a visible “continue at prior scope” option, use symmetric acceptance and refusal effort, avoid unrelated bundling, disclose material evidence ancestry, and record prompt frequency and defaults. High-risk rights may require a user-controlled or institutionally separate review surface.

nodes.label: Causal ancestry under compression
nodes.description: What minimum metadata preserves a material policy ancestor when agents summarize, aggregate, anonymize, or learn from evidence? Full traces threaten privacy; short provenance chains lose causal content.

nodes.label: Permission partial orders
nodes.description: How should systems compare scopes with budgets, recipient sets, purposes, time windows, and subdelegation? Which transitions are widening, narrowing, or incomparable without inventing arbitrary scalar weights?

nodes.label: Chosen formation
nodes.description: How can a grant distinguish a person choosing to be coached from a provider declaring “coaching” after the fact? What evidence of comprehension and refusal is proportionate?

nodes.label: Review independence
nodes.description: When is a review channel sufficiently separate from the beneficiary? Must a different institution ratify, or can a user-controlled interface suffice? How should the answer vary with risk?

nodes.label: Interference and collective authority
nodes.description: How should policy effects be estimated when one person's agent changes a household, team, market, or public environment? Who defines the target population and represents non-principals?

nodes.label: Strategic equilibria
nodes.description: Do ancestry-aware rules reduce influence expenditure, move it to unobserved channels, or cause agents to avoid useful responsibility? Which commitments are stable?

nodes.label: Real versus formal authority
nodes.description: Can an audit combine typed permissions with measures of knowledge dependence, switching cost, initiative, and institutional control without pretending they share a single scale?

nodes.label: Privacy-preserving audit
nodes.description: Can zero-knowledge proofs, secure computation, aggregation, or trusted execution show that an evidence path satisfies a policy without exposing intimate behavioral traces?

nodes.label: Artificial standing
nodes.description: How would governance change if a delegate could have morally relevant interests or a claim to continuity? Which authority and revocation concepts remain valid?

nodes.label: Cross-cultural validity
nodes.description: Which role and authority assumptions are culturally contingent? What participatory methods can specify local jurisdiction without freezing existing domination into code?

nodes.description: Automation can leave operators responsible for difficult exceptions while reducing routine practice.
